item.title: The Relationship Lessons Hidden in the Film, The Invite
item.description:
Relationships

The Relationship Lessons Hidden in the Film, The Invite

How silence, assumptions, and choice quietly shape lasting love.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional distance often develops through avoidance.
  • Lasting relationships require curiosity, repair, and intentional conversations.
  • The conversations couples avoid often become the conflicts they eventually face.

Relationships Don't Break Overnight

As therapists, we often say that relationships rarely end because of a single event. More often, they erode through countless moments of silence, assumptions, and emotional distance. The Invite captures this reality in a way that feels both intimate and unsettling. While the film unfolds around a seemingly ordinary invitation, it quickly becomes something much deeper: an exploration of what happens when people carry years of unspoken emotions into a room where honesty can no longer be postponed. The story is about everything that existed long before it.

When Assumptions Replace Curiosity

One of the most compelling themes in The Invite is that emotional disconnection is gradual. Couples often assume that love disappears first. In clinical practice, however, we frequently see the opposite. Love may still exist, but curiosity fades. Conversations become transactional. Partners stop asking meaningful questions because they believe they already know the answers.

Over time, assumptions replace discovery. Healthy relationships are built on the willingness to keep learning about one another. Our partners continue to grow, change, and evolve, and lasting intimacy requires us to stay curious rather than rely on outdated assumptions.

The Stories We Never Tell

Every person in the film carries a private narrative. Some are protecting themselves from rejection. Others are protecting the people they love. Many are protecting an identity they no longer know how to change.

From a systemic perspective, these untold stories are never purely individual. Every silence, every avoided conversation, and every hidden fear influences the entire relationship. When difficult conversations are postponed, tension does not disappear. Instead, it often reappears as criticism, emotional withdrawal, anxiety, resentment, or conflict over seemingly minor issues.

The conversation we avoid today often becomes tomorrow's crisis.

Love Is a Choice We Continue to Make

Perhaps the film's most important question is whether long-term relationships survive because people stay together—or because they repeatedly choose one another.

These are very different ideas.

Staying together can become passive.

Choosing each other is active.

Choosing means remaining curious. It means repairing after conflict, taking responsibility for our actions, and making space for our partner's changing experiences. It means recognizing that commitment is a decision renewed through everyday interactions.

Communication Is More Than Talking

The conversations throughout the film illustrate something therapists witness every day: people often communicate constantly without truly connecting. Communication is more than exchanging information. It is the willingness to say, "This is what I'm feeling." "This is what I'm afraid of." "This is what I need from you."

The greatest moments of intimacy often begin when someone finally says the words they have been rehearsing silently for years.

Relationships Sometimes Need a Fresh Beginning

One of the film's quiet but powerful messages is that relationships sometimes need to be restarted rather than maintained.

I often ask couples a simple question: "If you met your partner today, knowing everything you know now, how would you begin this relationship differently?"

The question is about possibility. Healthy relationships evolve because the people within them evolve. Trying to preserve an old version of the relationship often creates more suffering than allowing it to become something new.

Why Stories Matter

The renowned relationship therapist Esther Perel has observed that art can do things therapy cannot. Films invite us to recognize ourselves without the pressure of being analyzed. They create space for reflection, empathy, and emotional insight through story.

That is one reason cinema can be such a powerful complement to therapy. It carries ideas that often remain within classrooms and therapy offices into everyday culture, allowing people to reflect on their own relationships long before they seek professional help.

The Invite leaves us with a question worth considering: If the people we love truly heard the story we have been silently carrying, would they recognize us—and are we brave enough to let them?

Sometimes healing begins with having the conversation we have been postponing.

item.title: Listening to the Body
item.description:
Chronic Illness

Listening to the Body

Using interoception in chronic illness.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Interoception is the process of sensing, interpreting, integrating, and regulating body signals.
  • Interoception can be challenging when one lives with chronic illness.
  • Practicing interoception with attention to body sensations and emotions is key.
Source: Katie Willard Virant

Interoception is “a set of processes through which an organism senses, interprets, integrates, and regulates signals originating from within the body (Locatelli et al., 2023).” We use interoception all the time. For example, we sense that our eyelids are heavy and a yawn is coming on. We interpret these cues as fatigue. We look at the clock and note the late hour, causing us to integrate our body’s cues with our knowledge that bedtime is approaching. We regulate these signals by winding down for the night and going to bed. Note that the chain of activity here operates almost automatically.

Unfortunately, interoception is not always that seamless, especially when we live with chronic illness. Let’s take a look at the various steps of interoception, what gets in the way of performing those steps, and how we can strengthen our interoception abilities.

Listening to the Body

For many people living with illness, the body is the site of pain and mistrust. Understandably, detachment from the body occurs with the attitude “I’d prefer not to think about my body at all” predominating. In order to strengthen interoception skills, we need to move from detachment to reconnection. Our bodies have important information for us; if we’re not listening, we’re depriving ourselves of important data.

Reconnecting with the body begins with attention. You might begin by lying on a yoga mat or sitting in a comfortable chair. Use your breath as an anchor (O’Dowd & Griffith, 2022) and slowly follow your inhalations and exhalations. Notice your chest rising and falling. As you begin to feel more attuned to your body, you might try a body scan, moving attention from the top of your head to the tips of your toes.

Go slowly, just noticing how it feels to be in your body. Name sensations as you notice them: “My left shoulder feels tight. My chest feels relaxed and expansive. My lower abdomen is cramping. My feet are tingling." Remember that the body is the site of positive sensations, too — something that can be hard to remember when one lives with illness. Register these positive sensations during your body scan, allowing yourself to enjoy them.

If you’re new to this type of work, it may be difficult. You may feel bored, frustrated, or discouraged. Consistent practice is key. Starting small — even with one or two slowed breaths — is fine. You will build intensity and duration of attention as you continue to practice.

Emotional Responses to the Body

As you turn your attention to your body, you will notice that you also are having thoughts and feelings about the body sensations you are experiencing (Mehling et al., 2012). For example, you may feel alarm when you tune in to a painful sensation. You also may feel that it’s challenging to feel happiness when you tune into a positive sensation, as you have the thought that it’s only a matter of time before your body turns on you. Pay attention to these thoughts and feelings that come up, so you can understand and evaluate them. Often, our feelings arise not only from what is happening in the moment, but also from past experiences.

If you are noticing anxiety in response to body signals, ask yourself: “Am I feeling this level of anxiety because I’m in pain at this moment? Or am I feeling this anxious because I have felt pain in the past and am scared to feel it again?” Similarly, wonder about thoughts that dampen joy: “Am I afraid to feel at home in my body because of how it feels at this moment? Or because I’m remembering past experiences that are not occurring right now?”

Remember that the goal is not to eliminate emotional responses to body signals, but rather to understand and manage them. There’s no reason to say, “Darn it, there’s that pesky anxiety again. What’s wrong with me?” Instead, say something like, “This anxiety is larger than the current situation warrants. I understand why that is the case, but I want to see if I can turn it down to more appropriately reflect what is actually happening in this moment.”

Action Responses to the Body

Our body gives us data so that we can use it. Illness symptoms are often a sign that we need to take action. If we feel fatigue, is our body asking us to rest? If our muscles ache, will a heating pad feel soothing? If our symptoms seem to be flaring, is a call to the doctor in order? When we tune into our body, we are asking it, “What are you communicating to me? What do you need from me right now?”

Conclusion

To summarize, practicing interoception is (1) tuning in to bodily sensations; (2) tuning in to emotions and thoughts about those sensations; (3) adjusting where necessary by using compassionate self-talk to stay in the here-and-now; and (4) taking action to improve discomfort and pain. Psychotherapy can be a helpful space in which to learn and deepen interoception.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: When Should We Talk to Kids About Money?
item.description:
Child Development

When Should We Talk to Kids About Money?

Before children understand money, they understand contribution.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Children absorb money messages early.
  • Money talks can begin with contribution.
  • Helping builds confidence, agency, and belonging.
  • Silence can make money feel secretive or shameful.
Contributing to the family
Source: Ketut Subiyanto/Pexels

It’s summer break. For some children, this might include camp, tutoring, sports, and different kinds of enrichment activities many parents hope will benefit them in the future. For others, summer might be a child's first taste of entrepreneurship: a lemonade stand, garage sale, babysitting, or selling something homemade.

In my years of working with children and families, parents often ask: When is it time to talk to kids about money?

My answer is usually: earlier than you think, but perhaps not by starting with money.

For young children, money can be abstract, especially in our increasingly cashless society. They watch adults tap phones, swipe cards, or click buttons without fully understanding what is happening underneath. Money can also be emotionally loaded, especially in families where money narratives have been tied to stress, scarcity, conflict, guilt, or shame.

Some parents have shared with me their worries that talking about money too openly will spoil their children, make them entitled, or cause them to focus too much on superficial things. I remind parents that this concern makes sense. Most parents are trying to raise children who are grounded, generous, and aware that money is not the only measure of a life. But when families avoid money entirely, children may still learn something. They may learn that money is mysterious, dangerous, shameful, or too emotionally charged to discuss.

This is why I believe that money conversations do not need to begin with money itself. The better entry point may be contribution.

Contribution asks: How do I help? How do I participate in this family? What can I do that matters? How do I notice what is needed, offer effort, and feel proud of being useful?

How Children Develop Self-Confidence and Agency Through Helping

Long before children understand money as a system, they are learning whether they are capable. Developmental psychologist Erik Erikson described childhood as a time when children are working through autonomy, initiative, and eventually industry. Children are asking: Can I do things? Can I make choices? Am I useful here?

Any parent who has tried to leave the house with a young child knows this stage well. The child insists, “I do it myself,” while you mentally calculate how much faster it would be to do it for them. They want to pull on their own socks, pour the milk, crack the egg, stir the batter, or push the grocery cart, often at the exact moment when you are tired, rushed, or trying to avoid another mess.

And yet, when there is enough time and patience, something important happens. The milk may spill. The eggshells may fall into the bowl. The clothes may be mismatched. But then comes the look of satisfaction on their face: I did that myself.

That moment matters. The task may be small to the adult, but it is not small to the child. It becomes one of the early building blocks of mastery, self-confidence, and agency. The child experiences their own effort as meaningful.

This desire to help starts early. In their 2006 Science study, Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello found that children as young as 18 months would help adults achieve their goals in a variety of situations, even without reward. Helping is not something adults need to force into children. In many cases, it is something children are already reaching toward. They want to be included. They want to be a participant.

How Different Cultures Teach Children Responsibility Through Contribution

Cultural research adds another layer. Barbara Rogoff and colleagues have written about Learning by Observing and Pitching In, or LOPI, a way children learn by being included in the everyday activities of their families and communities. In the 2015 volume edited by Maricela Correa-Chávez, Rebeca Mejía-Arauz, and Barbara Rogoff, researchers describe how this form of learning is seen in many Indigenous communities of the Americas. Children are present for everyday work. They watch, they try, and over time they are trusted with more. They are expected to notice what is needed and gradually take on real responsibility.

I saw this firsthand during my time as a Peace Corps Volunteer in the rural highlands of Peru, where there was less differentiation between “child” tasks and “adult” tasks. There were community tasks: things that needed to be done to support the collective.

There was a four-year-old girl, Elena, who lived in a neighboring village. I always enjoyed seeing her and had a special fondness for her sunburnt cheeks and gapped smile. One morning before a workshop, we woke around 4 a.m. while it was still dark. The other participants and the horse had not arrived, so her father sent her down from their adobe house into the town square, where there was no electricity, to fetch the horse and round up the others.

I remember watching her run down the mountain with complete determination. Twenty minutes later, she returned with a few participants and the horse, beaming. I asked her father, “Wasn’t she afraid? It’s so dark.”

He told me, “She’s seen us do this many times. She’s helping.”

I do not share this story because I think every four-year-old should be sent into the dark to retrieve a horse. What stayed with me was the clarity of her role. Elena was contributing. She had observed the adults around her. She understood the task. She knew she had something to offer.

How Children Learn Value

So when families ask how to teach kids about money, I often help them consider a broader question: How do children learn value? Not just the value of a dollar, but the value of their effort, attention, time, and participation.

For a toddler, that might mean carrying napkins to the table, putting toys in a basket, or helping wipe up a spill. For a young child, it might mean sorting socks, choosing fruit at the store, or feeding the dog. For an older child or teenager, it might mean understanding the cost of an activity, saving toward something meaningful, planning a simple meal, comparing prices, or talking honestly about tradeoffs. Children begin to internalize that contribution is part of living in relationship with others.

I also remind families that money conversations are not a one-time thing. They unfold as children age, ask questions, compare themselves to peers or siblings, and wonder, “What is my place in this family?” and eventually, “What is my place in this world?”

When adults can talk about money with steadiness, children can begin to understand that money is part of life, but not the whole of life. It can be connected to effort, limits, choice, generosity, and responsibility. Children are not always listening to what we say, but they are constantly observing what we do. The goal is to create a family culture where money can be discussed without secrecy or shame, where contribution is expected, and where children learn that their effort, care, and participation matter.
